Divine Guidance
di-VYN GY-duhns
noun
The leading of God’s people in the way they should go, by His Word, providence, and Spirit; from the Latin divinus and the Old French guider, to lead.

Biblical Definition

Divine guidance is the gracious leading of God’s people in the way they should go—His direction of their steps by His Word, His providence, and His Spirit. Scripture is full of the promise: in all thy ways acknowledge Him, and He shall direct thy paths; I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go, I will guide thee with mine eye; thine ears shall hear a word behind thee, saying, This is the way, walk ye in it. The chief and sufficient means of guidance is the written Word—thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path—which makes plain the will of God in all things needful for faith and life. Where Scripture has not spoken to the particulars of a decision, God guides His people by sanctified wisdom drawn from the Word, by godly counsel, by the ordering of providence, and by the inward working of the Spirit conforming the heart to His will—never by new revelation added to the closed canon. The dictionary reads divine guidance as the believer’s confidence that the God who orders all things will lead His trusting child: not by voices and signs sought apart from Scripture, but by His Word as the lamp, His providence as the path, and His Spirit applying the Word—so that the man who acknowledges God in all his ways and leans not on his own understanding shall find his steps directed by a faithful and all-wise Guide.

Webster 1828 Definition

The gracious leading of God’s people in the way they should go, by His Word, providence, and Spirit; chiefly by the written Word as a lamp, never by new revelation.

Psa 32:8 — "I will instruct thee and teach thee in the way which thou shalt go: I will guide thee with mine eye."

Modern Corruption

Guidance is sought through subjective impressions, signs, and “words from the Lord” set beside or above Scripture; true guidance comes chiefly by the sufficient Word, with wisdom, counsel, and providence under it.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The corruption to name is the seeking of divine guidance through subjective impressions, signs, fleeces, and private “words from the Lord” set beside or above the Scripture. Much popular Christianity teaches believers to await an inner voice or mystical nudge for every decision, treating hunches as revelation and so opening the door to self-deception and to a guidance that bypasses the Word. But God does not lead His people by new revelations added to the closed canon; the man who governs his steps by impressions has no sure rule and is tossed by his own feelings dressed up as the Spirit’s voice.

The principle to recover is guidance chiefly by the sufficient Word. The Scripture is the lamp to the feet and the light to the path, making plain the will of God in all that is needful; where it has spoken, the believer obeys, and where it has not spoken to the particulars, God guides by sanctified wisdom drawn from the Word, by godly counsel, by the ordering of providence, and by the Spirit conforming the heart to His revealed will. The believer who acknowledges God in all his ways and leans not on his own understanding is promised a directed path—not by voices sought apart from Scripture, but by the faithful God who leads His trusting child through His Word and His providence.
